---
title: "Quiz: brightness constancy and the aperture problem"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Convention: $x$ to the right, $y$ down; the flow $(u, v)$ is in pixels per frame.

---

**Q1.** What does the optical flow at a pixel tell you, and how is it different from the single shift found by FFT registration?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One vector per image, or one per pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The flow at a pixel is the vector from where its content is in frame 1 to where it is in frame 2. FFT registration finds one translation for the whole image; optical flow finds a vector for every pixel, so different parts of the image can move differently (a crawling cell over a still background, a rotating embryo).
:::

---

**Q2.** In a colour-wheel picture of a flow field, a region is white and another is a saturated blue. What do you know about the two regions? What else do you need to know to give their speeds in pixels per frame?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Saturation encodes speed, but relative to what?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
White means (almost) still. Saturated blue means moving fast in the direction that the wheel colours blue (with red = right and the hue running counter-clockwise, blue is roughly down-left on screen). Saturation is relative to the largest speed of the colour scale, so you need the scale ("edge of the wheel = 2 px/frame") to turn it into a speed.
:::

---

**Q3.** Name three situations in fluorescence time-lapse imaging where brightness constancy fails. What does a flow method report there?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Anything that changes the grey value of a point that does not move.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Photobleaching (everything dims each frame), blinking fluorophores, objects moving in or out of the focal plane, a change of illumination or focus drift. A flow method explains every change of grey value as motion, so it reports spurious motion (for example a bias along the slopes of a bleaching spot), or misses true motion.
:::

---

**Q4.** In 1D, a pixel has slope $I_x = 4$ and its value drops by 6 from frame 1 to frame 2. Estimate the motion. What can you say about a pixel with $I_x = 0$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$u = -I_t / I_x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$I_t = -6$, so $u = -(-6)/4 = 1.5$ pixels per frame to the right. At $I_x = 0$ (a flat stretch or a peak) the equation reads $0 \cdot u = -I_t$: it says nothing about $u$. Such a pixel needs help from its neighbours.
:::

---

**Q5.** In a kymograph ($x$ across, time down) you see a vertical line, a line tilted to the right and two lines crossing. Interpret them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How far does a feature move per frame on each line?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Vertical: a feature that does not move. Tilted to the right: a feature moving right, with speed = horizontal change per frame (the slope). Crossing lines: two features passing each other (for example vesicles moving in opposite directions along an axon).
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can you not measure the motion of a long straight edge from a small window, however carefully you look? What part of the motion can you measure?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Slide the edge along itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sliding the edge along itself does not change any pixel in the window, so motion along the edge is invisible: this is the aperture problem. Only the component across the edge (along the gradient), the normal flow, can be measured.
:::

---

**Q7.** In velocity space, pixel A's constraint is the line $u = 2$, pixel B's is $v = 1$. A third pixel C, on the same edge as A, gives $u = 2$ again. What is the motion? What if only A and C were available?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do the lines cross?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A and B cross at $(u, v) = (2, 1)$; C lies on A's line and adds nothing new. With only A and C (both on the same edge) all we know is $u = 2$: any $v$ fits. The point of the line closest to the origin, $(2, 0)$, is the normal flow.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Derive the optical flow constraint from brightness constancy. Which term is dropped, and when is that safe?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
First-order Taylor expansion in $x$, $y$ and $t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$I(x + u, y + v, t + 1) = I(x, y, t)$. Expanding to first order: $I + I_x u + I_y v + I_t = I$, so $I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0$. Dropped: the second-order terms ($\tfrac12 I_{xx}u^2 + I_{xy}uv + \dots$). Safe when the motion is small compared with the distance over which the gradient changes (about a pixel at the scale of the image structure); for larger motion the next unit uses warping and pyramids.
:::
